title: Data Distribution
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and main trade-off of data distribution.
Apply data distribution to a small MongoDB data or operational scenario.
Verify the expected result, one edge case, and the relevant version/deployment assumption.

content.intro: Learn data distribution as part of Sharding and Horizontal Scaling. The lesson preserves the PDF subtopics, connects them to a practical MongoDB pattern, and ends with a verification task.
content.why_it_matters: Data Distribution affects how MongoDB distributes data and routes queries. Evaluate candidate shard keys against real cardinality, write patterns, query targeting and growth; poor distribution can create hotspots even in a large cluster.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with the behavior you want, identify the collection/document shape and access pattern involved, then select the smallest MongoDB operation that expresses the requirement. Define the consistency requirement and retry policy, then rehearse failure and recovery in a controlled environment.

content_blocks.expected_output: In a sharded cluster, the shell summarizes sharding configuration; standalone deployments do not provide this cluster context.
content_blocks.run_instructions: CodeLeaf displays this example as a reference and does not execute a MongoDB server or arbitrary driver code in the page. Run shell examples with mongosh, or driver examples in a separately configured Node.js/Python lab, against a disposable database. Verify installed server/driver versions and deployment feature availability first. Never place credentials in source files.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a dedicated training database and synthetic fixtures. Remove only objects created by this lesson or recreate the disposable database after confirming the target; do not run destructive/reset commands against production.

content_blocks.title: Environment and safety note
content_blocks.text: All examples are teaching references, not production-ready configuration. MongoDB Atlas-specific Search, Vector Search, monitoring, backup and automation features are marked as deployment-dependent. Server, driver, shell and managed-service capabilities differ; check the official documentation that matches your target.

content.task: Try it yourself: Compare candidate shard keys against cardinality, write distribution and query targeting; use a workload table to identify hotspots and unbounded scatter-gather queries. Submit your choice plus the expected result/evidence and one edge case.
task_acceptance_criteria: Demonstrate the key idea in Data Distribution.
Predict the result and state how you would verify it.
Name one boundary, risk or version/deployment assumption.
hints: First, explain what “Data Distribution” needs to accomplish in this scenario.
Write down the data shape, filter, expected output or operational evidence before running the example.
Test one normal case and one meaningful boundary/failure case; consult the matching official reference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming distributed operations succeed instantly and always once
common_mistakes.why: Retries, failover, lag and multi-document boundaries can affect observable behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Define the consistency requirement and retry policy, then rehearse failure and recovery in a controlled environment.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a static reference result proves the environment will behave identically.
common_mistakes.why: MongoDB server, shell, driver, managed service and permissions can affect the available behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Record the target versions and privileges, run the smallest safe test, and keep expected and actual results side by side.

summary: Data Distribution affects how MongoDB distributes data and routes queries. Evaluate candidate shard keys against real cardinality, write patterns, query targeting and growth; poor distribution can create hotspots even in a large cluster.
